title: Thermodynamics and chemical equilibrium
summary: Whether a reaction goes: enthalpy from bond enthalpies, enthalpies of formation and Hess's law with standard states and phases stated; entropy and the second law; Gibbs free energy, spontaneity and its temperature dependence; dynamic equilibrium, the reaction quotient and the equilibrium constant, ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q and ΔG° = −RT ln K; ICE-table calculations and Le Châtelier's principle argued through Q and K.

objectives.description: Compute ΔH° for a reaction from enthalpies of formation and estimate it from mean bond enthalpies, and explain the discrepancy in terms of phases and averaging.
Predict the sign of ΔS° and compute it from absolute entropies; compute ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° and decide spontaneity under standard conditions at a stated temperature.
Find the temperature at which a reaction's spontaneity changes, stating the assumption that ΔH° and ΔS° are temperature-independent.
Write Q and K with their reference states, relate ΔG° to K, decide the direction of change from Q versus K, and solve an ICE-table equilibrium problem.
Predict and explain the response of an equilibrium to changes of concentration, pressure, inert gas, catalyst and temperature, distinguishing what changes K from what changes Q.

preparation.description: OpenStax 5.3 Enthalpy: first law, state functions, standard state (1 bar, 1 M), enthalpy of formation, Hess's law (Examples 5.8–5.15); skim 5.1–5.2 if heat and calorimetry are new.
Lecture 15 notes pages 1–4: bond enthalpies, ΔHr° from bond enthalpies and from heats of formation, Hess's law.
OpenStax 16.2 Entropy and 16.3 The Second and Third Laws (Examples 16.2–16.6).
OpenStax 16.4 Free Energy: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, temperature dependence, ΔG° = −RT ln K (Examples 16.7–16.13), with lecture 16 notes pages 1–4.
Lecture 16 notes page 1: spontaneous change and ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; endothermic spontaneous processes.
OpenStax 13.1 Chemical Equilibria and 13.2 Equilibrium Constants: dynamic equilibrium, Q, Kc and Kp, heterogeneous equilibria (Examples 13.1–13.5).
Lecture 18 notes page 2: ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q, ΔG° = −RT ln K, direction from Q versus K.
OpenStax 13.4 Equilibrium Calculations (ICE tables; Examples 13.6–13.10) and 13.3 Le Châtelier's Principle.

For every quantity with a ° write in the notebook what the standard state is and at which temperature the value holds; for every equation write the phase of each species. activities.title: Tutorial: enthalpy two ways and spontaneity with temperature
activities.instructions: Attempt exercises 1 and 2 before asking for hints. Write the balanced equation with phases first, state the temperature and standard state you are using, and carry units (kJ versus J) explicitly; the commonest error in this unit is a factor of 1000 in TΔS.

activities.title: Problem class: reading an equilibrium
activities.instructions: Exercise 3. Set up the ICE table in full and check your equilibrium pressures by substituting back into K before you interpret anything.

activities.title: Explain: ΔG versus ΔG°
activities.instructions: Without the notes, write five sentences in the notebook on the difference between ΔG and ΔG°, which one is zero at equilibrium, and why K depends only on temperature. Compare with lecture 18 pages 1–2.

activities.title: Retrieval: the unit's relations
activities.instructions: From memory: ΔHr° from ΔHf°; the bond-enthalpy estimate and its sign convention; ΔG = ΔH − TΔS and the four sign cases; ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q; ΔG° = −RT ln K; what shifts an equilibrium and what changes K.

commonMisconceptions.claim: Exothermic reactions are spontaneous and endothermic ones are not.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Spontaneity at constant T and P is decided by ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. Ice melts above 0 °C and ammonium nitrate dissolves although both are endothermic, because TΔS outweighs ΔH (lecture 16, pages 1–2).

commonMisconceptions.claim: Bond enthalpies give the exact enthalpy of reaction.
commonMisconceptions.correction: They are averages over many gaseous molecules and apply to gas-phase bonds only; a condensed-phase product adds its enthalpy of condensation. Enthalpies of formation are specific to each compound and phase (lecture 15, pages 2–3).
ΔG = 0 at equilibrium. ΔG° is a fixed number for the reaction at a given temperature, related to K by ΔG° = −RT ln K; it is zero only in the special case K = 1 (lecture 18, page 2).

commonMisconceptions.claim: Adding a reactant or compressing the mixture changes K.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Those stresses change Q, and the system moves until Q equals the unchanged K. Only temperature changes K, in the direction fixed by the sign of ΔH° (lecture 18, pages 4–5; lecture 19).
